I bet it is not culling through reams of dense documents, agendas, minutes, legal docs. We've all been there, but there's a way to make it easier. Let's talk about skills. A ChatGPT skill is a reusable workflow that tells ChatGPT or Codex how to do a specific task the same way every time. It can include instructions, examples, and even code if you're technical like that, so you don't have to rebuild the same prompt or re-explain the newsroom standard every time. Skills are great for repeatable work where consistency matters. The same steps, the same kind of input, the same kind of output. Think weekly agenda scans, source follow-up checklists, public record reviews, or internal editor prep packets. Skills can also be shared across the team. So instead of every reporter inventing their own process, the newsroom can capture one approved workflow and reuse it. Everybody still writes in their own voice. The skill just gives them the same clean starting point. It's perfect when your newsroom needs the same input turned into the same output every single time. For the demo, let's make a skill for a weekly city council agenda scan. This is a great use of a skill. Help a local reporter review a public meeting agenda or packet. This means a new reporter, producer, or editor begins from the same starting point. People still write in their own voice. This just gives everybody a leg up. Quick reality check. Do not store privileged information in a skill unless your organization has signed off. A skill is not policy. It's not legal review. It's not a golden ticket to publish. Everything still needs a human in the loop. But the value is in repeating what is repeatable. If the newsroom does something every week, and the steps are clear, a skill can make that routine work a little less chaotic. Ultimately, skills are great because they're boring in the best possible way. They let journalists spend less time rebuilding process and more time doing journalism.
